clue.text: "Odd lad", whined Snow White, "starting to disrupt the talk pointlessly"

indicators.note: to disrupt is to throw into disorder, so the gathered letters are rearranged
the odd-numbered letters of lad, the first and third, are taken

parts.note: taken as written into the pool
taken as written into the pool

indicators.note: only the starting letter of the word to is used

explanation.surface: A grumbling Snow White complains that a strange boy is starting to interrupt the chat with pointless talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' takes L and D from lad, 'starting' takes T from to, and 'disrupt' shuffles them with WHINED and SNOWWHITE. The quoted speech makes whined look like a verb of saying, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to speak to no purpose, an old sense recorded alongside letting something go.

clue.text: Half of bitter is, in practice, weak

indicators.note: one piece sits in the middle of the other, splitting the word for practice

parts.note: a way is a habit or practice, as in 'the way we do things'

indicators.note: the second half of the word bitter is taken, its last three letters

explanation.surface: A beer drinker complains that their bitter, in practice, is only half strength.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Half of bitter' as a half-pint of beer; it is half of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Watery is a synonym for weak, said of thin drinks diluted too far.

clue.text: Inauguration of popular Democrat not starting a commotion

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable

indicators.note: the word for a commotion loses its starting letter

parts.note: a ruction is a noisy disturbance or row

explanation.surface: A popular Democrat's swearing-in begins without any commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not starting' cuts the R from RUCTION, leaving UCTION.
explanation.definitionFit: An induction is the formal installation of someone into office, much as an inauguration is.

clue.text: Go on site regularly for meeting

parts.note: to have a go is to try

indicators.note: every other letter of site is taken, the first and third

explanation.surface: A worker is told to visit the site at regular intervals for a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes S and T from site.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a meeting, usually a secret romantic appointment between lovers.

clue.text: Long time to bank old money with one for guidance

indicators.note: to bank is to hold safely, so the long time holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long period
a ducat is an old gold coin used across Europe
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Advice to bank old money for a long time, with one person giving guidance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' looks like depositing money, but 'to bank' means to hold the other pieces inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Education is instruction or teaching, the guidance given to learners.

clue.text: See 1 across
Condition after last of bread; toasted maybe?

indicators.note: the condition word comes after the bread's letter
only the final letter of the word bread is used

parts.note: rank means standing or condition, as in social rank

explanation.surface: A kitchen question: the state of the last of the bread, toasted perhaps?
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads toasted as grilled bread; in fact it means drank someone's health, a toast being one example of drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: To toast someone is to raise a glass and drink, so toasted is an example of the past tense of drinking.

clue.text: Healthy measure for daughter not a moment too soon

parts.note: well means in good health
time in music is the measure or metre of a piece

explanation.surface: A healthy dose measured out for a daughter arrives just in time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something well-timed comes at just the right moment, neither early nor late; the clue's phrase is an idiom for that.

clue.text: Herb gets the no. 4 to Scarborough Fair

definitions.meaning: a culinary plant used for seasoning
the folk song's refrain lists parsley, sage, rosemary and then a fourth herb

explanation.surface: A herb rides the number four bus to the Scarborough fair.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a bus route; the song 'Scarborough Fair' repeats 'parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme', and this is the fourth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is an aromatic garden herb, the last of the four named in the song's famous refrain.

clue.text: In Sheffield estate, has been around the longest

indicators.note: the letters sit within the phrase Sheffield estate, spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A resident of a Sheffield housing estate has lived there longest.
explanation.definitionFit: The eldest is the oldest of a group, the one who has existed for the most time.

clue.text: Now father's taken in by flirt

indicators.note: the word for father is held within the word for flirt

parts.note: to toy with someone is to flirt or trifle with them
da is an informal word for father; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Dad has just been fooled by a flirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sense of being fooled hides the containment signalled by 'taken in by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Today, used as an adverb, means at the present time, just as now does.

clue.text: You end up including everything pure

indicators.note: the mixed letters hold the word for everything within them
up here means stirred up, so the letters of you end are mixed

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: You finish up taking in everything that is pure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads as a direction but means stirred up, mixing the letters to UNOYED before 'including' takes in the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Unalloyed literally describes metal not mixed with another, and so figuratively means pure or complete.

clue.text: Car racket broken up in Newmarket

definitions.note: the definition names a place where one is found rather than a synonym

indicators.note: the letters are broken apart and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A noisy car is broken up in the Suffolk town of Newmarket.
explanation.walkthrough: Newmarket, in Suffolk, is the home of British horse racing, with a famous course.
explanation.definitionFit: Newmarket has a celebrated horse-racing course, so a circuit for racing is found in that town.

clue.text: Elite ensemble comprising 14-19 year olds

indicators.note: the phrase elite ensemble contains the letters within it, across the word break

explanation.surface: An elite music ensemble made up of adolescents aged fourteen to nineteen.
explanation.definitionFit: Teenagers are people aged thirteen to nineteen, so the age range given falls among them.

clue.text: See 1 across
The most bent new depositor

indicators.note: a new arrangement of the letters of depositor is made

explanation.surface: The most crooked figure is a newly arrived depositor at the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' suggests crooked or dishonest, but here it means sagging.
explanation.definitionFit: Droopiest describes whatever sags or hangs down the most, bent over furthest.

clue.text: As Panama is first to greet King and Scotsman

parts.note: 1st is the abbreviation of first, with the digit read as the letter I
HM stands for His Majesty, a king
Ian is a typically Scottish first name, a crossword stand-in for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: Someone first greets a king and then a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to greet' and 'and' simply join the pieces, IST, HM and IAN, in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Panama is an isthmus, a narrow neck of land between seas, so it is isthmian in character.

clue.text: Farm vehicle mostly capable, easy to control

indicators.note: most of the farm vehicle's name is used, dropping its end

parts.note: a tractor is the standard farm vehicle
able means capable

explanation.surface: A farm vehicle that is mostly capable and easy to handle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts the last two letters OR from TRACTOR, leaving TRACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tractable describes someone or something docile, easily managed or led.

clue.text: Serum not supporting animal shrouded by metal

parts.note: anti means against, not in favour of

indicators.note: the animal is wrapped inside the metal

parts.note: tin is a metal
an ox is an animal

explanation.surface: A serum, not backing an animal, is wrapped in metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shrouded by' signals the animal wrapped inside the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: An antitoxin is an antibody serum given to neutralise a poison in the body.

clue.text: What can put off a productive retirement?

definitions.text: What can put off a productive retirement?

parts.words: What can put off a productive retirement?
parts.note: retirement here is going to bed; a productive retirement is a good night's sleep, and the condition prevents it

explanation.surface: A question about what might spoil a fruitful life after work.
explanation.walkthrough: Retirement suggests leaving a job, but it means retiring for the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Insomnia is inability to sleep, which stops a night in bed from being restful.

clue.text: Ideal team will regularly produce the facts

indicators.note: every second letter of ideal team is taken, starting from the second

explanation.surface: A perfect team will consistently produce the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Data are facts and figures gathered for reference or analysis.

clue.text: Run between office assistants for quite a distance!

indicators.note: the run goes between the two assistants' abbreviations

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant and a sec is a secretary
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A dash between two office assistants covers a long way.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark points to the understatement: the unit is astronomically large.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsec is an astronomical unit, about 3.26 light years, certainly a long way.

clue.text: New cast at university behaves badly

indicators.note: a new arrangement of the letters of cast

parts.note: up means at university, as in up at Oxford

explanation.surface: A newly cast student production at university misbehaves.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'up' is a British idiom for being in residence at a university.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is an idiom for misbehaving or playing up.

clue.text: Storyteller adopts a retrograde stance

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the word for stance is read backwards

parts.note: a pose is a stance or posture

explanation.surface: A storyteller takes up an old-fashioned, reactionary position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrograde' looks like a political adjective for the stance but signals reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek teller of fables such as the tortoise and the hare.

clue.text: Artificial opening for most of the corporation

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, the end trimmed off

parts.note: corporation is a humorous old word for a pot belly

explanation.surface: An artificial opening has been created for most of the company.
explanation.walkthrough: Corporation looks like a company but is old slang for a paunch; 'most of' drops CH from STOMACH.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoma is a surgically made opening in the body, as in a colostomy.

clue.text: Girl goes somewhere cold — not twice — for cleansing

parts.note: Cath is a girl's name, short for Catherine

indicators.note: one of the two copies of a repeated letter is lost, so it appears only once

parts.note: the Arctic is a famously cold region

explanation.surface: A girl travels somewhere cold, though not a second time, for a detox.
explanation.walkthrough: ARCTIC has two Cs; 'not twice' keeps only one, giving ARTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathartic means purging or purifying, whether emotionally or physically, so it is cleansing.

clue.text: Group traps one in endless routine

indicators.note: the numeral goes inside the trimmed word for routine
the word for routine loses its final letter

parts.note: a chore is a routine task
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gang locks a person into a never-ending daily routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims CHORE to CHOR, and 'in' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir is a group of singers performing together.

clue.text: Religious senior gives some bother to Jack

indicators.note: the piece of bother is joined on to the end of the sailor

parts.note: a jack is a sailor, and AB, able seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: only some of the word bother is used, its last letters left off

explanation.surface: A senior monk causes trouble for a man called Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbot is the head of a monastery, a senior figure in a religious order.

clue.text: Small donkey a flop when it comes clouding the issue

definitions.note: the device is described by what it does, clouding a scene

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
moke is British slang for a donkey
a bomb is a total failure, a flop

explanation.surface: A small donkey proves a flop when it muddies matters.
explanation.walkthrough: MOKE is British slang for a donkey. The definition is a description: the device clouds things, literally with smoke and figuratively as a distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: A smoke bomb emits a thick cloud, and figuratively the term means a diversion that obscures the real matter.

clue.text: See 28
Lots talking about Bach sextet — or something else

indicators.note: the letters become something else, a different arrangement

explanation.surface: People gossiping about a Bach sextet, or some other piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'something else' shuffles the twelve letters of BACH SEXTET OR.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatterboxes are people who talk incessantly, so they are a lot who go on talking about things.

clue.text: Finished? That's def!

parts.note: deaf with its A consumed becomes def, so the clue words show a letter that has been devoured

explanation.surface: A slangy exclamation: is it over? Definitely!
explanation.walkthrough: Def looks like slang for definitely, but it is the word deaf with its A gone, consumed.
explanation.definitionFit: Eaten up means consumed entirely, so all finished, as when a meal has disappeared.
